title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, Risk & Exceptions
author: Priya Nair
content:
Summary:
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's authoritative guidance for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging standards, data residency and retention policy, secure SDLC expectations, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and the formal risk & exception process. It is intended for security, infra, platform, and product teams who operate customer-facing systems or manage client data and compliance artifacts.

1) Scope and intent
- Scope: applies to all Redwood-managed control plane components, hosted inference services, Dedicated control plane, Private deployments where Redwood provides the control plane, and all supporting infrastructure (identity, logging, KMS).
- Intent: define minimum controls, retention and evidence requirements for audits, and a repeatable risk/exception process that preserves security posture.

2) RBAC & Authentication (AuthN/AuthZ)
Overview:
- Primary identity provider: Keycloak (hosted by Redwood) for internal services and staff (SSO).
- Customer-facing API auth: API keys + OAuth2 client credentials for service-to-service.
- Device and machine identities: short-lived certs issued by our internal PKI (Vault PKI backend).

Role model and least privilege:
- Role matrix (high-level):
| Role | Scope | Can: read | Can: write | Can: admin |
|-----|-------|----------:|-----------:|----------:|
| viewer | project / org | yes | no | no |
| developer | service / env | yes | yes (non-prod only) | no |
| oncall | service / prod | yes | limited write (incidents) | no |
| infra-admin | infra | yes | yes | limited |
| security-admin | org | yes | yes | yes |

- Privilege separation: production write/admin operations require MFA + bastion session via Privileged Access Service (Teleport).
- Time-bound elevations: just-in-time (JIT) elevation is used for emergency changes; max duration 4 hours and must be recorded in the elevation ticket.

Authentication hardening:
- All human users: SSO + MFA (hardware tokens or TOTP).
- Service accounts: short-lived OAuth2 tokens with rotation every 7 days; long-lived API keys are prohibited except for customer-managed keys documented and justified.
- Secrets storage: HashiCorp Vault (transit/kv) with KMS/HSM wrapping for production keys.

Ownership and SLAs:
- RBAC policy owner: security-team (primary), eng-platform (secondary).
- Access request SLA: 48 hours for standard requests; 4 hours for emergency oncall escalations.

3) Audit logging standards
Goals: ensure actionable, tamper-evident logs for authentication, authorization, admin activity, deployment changes, and data access.

Sources to capture:
- Identity events: successful/failed logins, MFA challenges, token issuance/refresh, JIT elevations.
- Control plane API: create/update/delete for models, routes, keys, project configs.
- Infrastructure changes: Terraform apply, AMI builds, kube-apiserver admin calls.
- Data access: customer data exports, blob read/write where applicable.
- Incidents & escalation notes.

Log pipeline and storage:
- Collection: Fluent Bit -> central Kafka -> processing -> S3 (raw) + Splunk index (searchable).
- Integrity: logs signed at ingest with KMS-derived keys; reingestion rejected if signature mismatch.
- Retention tiers:
  - Security-critical audit logs (authN/authZ, admin): 7 years (S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year).
  - Operational logs (runtime traces, metrics): 90 days in Splunk, 1 year archived in S3.
  - Application debug logs: 30 days.

SLOs and thresholds:
- Audit ingestion latency: 99% of events indexed within 60s.
- Missing log detection: weekly job that asserts expected event volume per service; alerts if deviation >30%.

Access and monitoring:
- Only security-admins and designated auditors have read access to full auth logs; access is audited.
- Redaction: logs must not contain raw plaintext PII (API keys, secrets, SSNs). When PII is required for troubleshooting, use secure session capture available to security for time-limited review.

4) Data residency and retention policy
Residency model:
- Default storage regions: US (us-east-1) and EU (eu-west-1). Customer data resides in region selected at project creation.
- Cross-region replication: disabled by default for customer-controlled projects; enabled only with explicit customer consent and documented configuration.

Data classification & retention:
- Classification levels: public, internal, sensitive (PII), regulated (GDPR/CCPA/UK/DE requirements).
- Minimum retention by data class (examples):
  - Regulated customer data (exports, transcripts containing PII): retained per customer contract; default 7 years / per-local-regulation.
  - Audit logs (see Audit section): 7 years for security-critical.
  - Backups (snapshots): 90 days for ephemeral data, 365 days when requested by customer SLA.
  - Telemetry/metrics: 2 years (aggregated), raw telemetry 90 days.

Data deletion and customer requests:
- Right-to-be-forgotten: documented flow that coordinates product, security, and legal. Deletion includes database tombstones, blob deletes, and background recompact where appropriate; verifiable deletion evidence produced by automated job.
- Data export: exports must be encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest (AES-256). KMS keys used should be region-bound when the customer has residency requirements.

Ownership:
- Data residency owner: privacy-team and security (joint). Legal involvement required for regulated customers.

5) Secure SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle)
Minimum requirements by phase:
- Design: threat model created for all services tagged high/new (templates in eng-security repo); privacy impact assessment (PIA) for anything handling regulated data.
- Development: include static analysis (SAST) on every PR, dependency scanning (OSV/Snyk), and pre-commit checks for secrets.
- Review & test: mandatory design review for high-impact changes and mandatory code review by at least one reviewer not on the author's team for prod-affecting changes.
- CI/CD: pipeline runs unit tests, integration tests, SCA, and policy checks. Production deploys require signed artifacts and an automated canary stage.
- Release: release notes must include risk/rollback plan and security checklist.
- Production monitoring: new services must have health, error, and security telemetry defined before rollout.

Tooling and gates:
- Required tools: GitHub + branch protection, GitHub Actions CI with the security workflow, Snyk/Dependabot, HashiCorp Vault for secrets, image scanning (Trivy), and build artifact signing.
- Gate: policy-as-code prevents merges if SCA or SAST finds critical issues; exceptions must be approved via the risk/exception process.

6) Incident response (security) procedures
High-level runbook:
1. Detection & Triage: Security monitoring alerts -> pager to oncall sec responder. Triage within 15 minutes and declare incident severity (P0/P1/P2).
2. Containment: work with infra and platform to isolate affected services (traffic reroutes, revoke compromised keys).
3. Forensic capture: preserve logs and snapshots; increase log retention for affected services; create an immutable evidence bundle preserved in secure S3 with restricted access and a cryptographic hash.
4. Communication: follow internal comms playbook. External disclosure coordinated with legal and PR; customers notified within SLA in customer contracts.
5. Remediation & Recovery: apply fixes, run verification tests, and schedule post-incident rollout with canary.
6. Postmortem: 72-hour preliminary triage notes, full postmortem within 14 days listing root cause, remediation, timeline, and owner assignments.

Special procedures (data exposure):
- Immediate key revocation and rotation for affected keys.
- Customer data exposures: notify impacted customers per contract and legal jurisdiction requirements; preserve evidence for regulator review.

Evidence preservation and chain of custody:
- Evidence bundle details: signed archive (S3 path), manifest (JSON) with event hashes, list of owners, and access ACLs.
- Chain of custody: every access to the bundle is recorded in an access audit table and requires an access justification ticket.

7) Compliance evidence workflows
Audit readiness checklist:
- Owners mapped for each control (technical owner + evidence owner).
- Evidence types: screenshots, logs (with hashes), configuration exports (Terraform state), PKI manifests, access review spreadsheets, training attestations.
- Evidence retention: match control retention (usually 3-7 years depending on regulator).

Routine evidence collection (quarterly)
1. Evidence runbook kickoff: compliance manager triggers evidence collection job.
2. Automated artifacts: export Terraform state, S3 snapshot of policy docs, access-control report from Keycloak, signed log manifests from Splunk/S3.
3. Manual artifacts: manager attestations, policy sign-offs, and interview notes.
4. Package & review: security validates package, stores in compliance-evidence repository (secure S3), and notifies auditors.

On-demand evidence (customer/regulator request):
- Triage request, route to evidence owner, collect automated artifacts within 48 hours and manual artifacts within 5 business days unless extended by legal.

8) Risk & exception process
Purpose: allow documented, time-limited deviations from standards with compensating controls while preserving auditability.
Process steps:
1. Submit exception request (Confluence template): includes scope, risk assessment, compensating controls, duration, and rollback plan.
2. Security review: initial response within 3 business days.
3. Risk committee: for high-risk items, committee meeting within 7 business days (security, infra, product, legal).
4. Decision: approve (with controls), approve temporary (max 90 days), or deny.
5. Continuous monitoring: exceptions are tracked in the risk register; automated monitors (where possible) feed alerting for the scope.

Compensating controls examples:
- If cross-region replication is required but data residency restricts it: encrypt with region-bound KMS and require customer opt-in + additional logging + restricted access.
- If a legacy service cannot rotate keys immediately: require IP restrictions, reduce token TTL, and schedule remediation sprint within 30 days.

9) Ownership & governance
- Document owner: security-team (Priya Nair).
- Review cadence: annual full review and ad-hoc updates on major platform changes.
- Training: mandatory security & privacy training for engineers (annual), oncall tabletop exercises (quarterly).

10) Appendix: quick reference commands and examples
- Generate signed evidence manifest (example CLI):
  curl -X POST "https://evidence.internal.redwood/api/v1/package" -H "Authorization: Bearer $EVID_TOKEN" -d '{"services": ["control-plane","auth"], "range": "2026-02-01:2026-03-01" }'

- Sample permission XACML-like policy (pseudo-YAML):
  - policy: allow-dev-deploy
    effect: allow
    principals: [group:developers]
    actions: [deploy:create, deploy:update]
    resources: [env:staging]
